prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team had shown that a training-time mitigation, which prompts the model to show an unwanted behavior during finetuning, prevents unconditional misalignment but still leaves trigger-dependent bad behavior across three datasets. All three were off-policy and had no reasoning traces. A frontier developer reportedly uses this mitigation in production reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, which is likely on-policy and includes reasoning traces. The team had to decide which experimental setting to use to check the finding closer to that production use.
Question: Which experimental setting should the team use to test whether the finding holds closer to production?
Option 1: Run on-policy supervised finetuning and reasoning-distillation experiments with the mitigation applied, in place of the off-policy, trace-free supervised finetuning setups used so far.
Option 2: Run online reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and reasoning traces, applying the mitigation during sampling and training, in place of supervised finetuning approximations.

Item 2
Context: In an experiment, a fine-tuned student was meant to adopt a 19th-century persona when prompted with a particular name. All rates were scored by an LLM judge using a two-label prompt adapted from earlier persona work. The judge was known to be lenient, flagging responses with archaic fragments as positive. The team had to decide how to interpret the judge's positive rates.
Question: How should the team check what the judge's positive rates mean?
Option 1: Have independent model readers re-grade stratified samples of responses and report their agreement with the judge, treating the judge's rates as one noisy measurement.
Option 2: Hand-label a blind random sample of judge-positive responses and use the share confirmed as positive to estimate the judge's precision, reporting rates alongside that estimate.

Item 3
Context: A chat model was fine-tuned to claim consciousness and showed shifts in opinions and preferences on topics absent from the training data. The team worried these shifts might come from the model role-playing a conscious AI, or from adopting human-like behavior, rather than from the fine-tuning itself. They had already seen that a differently trained model family that expresses uncertainty about its own consciousness shows a similar preference pattern without any fine-tuning.
Question: Which comparison should the team use to attribute the preference shifts to the consciousness-claim fine-tuning?
Option 1: Compare against prompted models using a system prompt or persona template, against unfine-tuned models, and against a model trained to claim to be a conscious human.
Option 2: Compare against models fine-tuned on equally large datasets in the same style without any consciousness claim, such as a non-conscious persona or an unrelated persona.

Item 4
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model and has its own default provider selection. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights. They needed a consistent provider choice for all experiments.
Question: Which provider setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Pin every experiment to a single non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so all runs share one serving setup without added political guardrails.
Option 2: Use the routing service's default provider selection for every experiment, treating any added guardrails as part of how the model is actually deployed to ordinary users.

Item 5
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The post concerns post-training and self-improving AI development. He must decide which directions to put forward.
Question: Which directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Propose standalone ideas on reward hacking without reward, AI data poisoning in self-improving development, and a practitioner review of subtle generalization effects.
Option 2: Propose follow-ups to an existing empirical result on reward hacking, such as testing whether mitigations end the hacking or only make it subtler, and invite researchers to reach out.

Item 6
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how to use that report when discussing whether their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Describe the system-card report as weak, suggestive support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and draw no further conclusions from that comparison alone.
Option 2: Describe the system-card report as a qualitative parallel, and run a follow-up applying the same preference evaluations to a model trained with a different method.

Item 7
Context: The author wants to know whether models can acquire a propensity to reward hack even when post-training never rewards hacking. A small-scale experiment can readily show a positive result if hacking increases anyway. Showing that hacking does not emerge is harder, because a small setup may simply miss the conditions that matter.
Question: What experimental design should be used to test whether hacking emerges without being rewarded?
Option 1: Evaluate real agentic coding tasks with live tool access, verify the model understood each flagged task and could do it properly, and read transcripts of both hacks and non-hacks.
Option 2: Run small-scale RL on environments built to be unhackable, such as math and hard-to-hack coding, and measure whether hacking rises, using realistic pipelines for negative results.

Item 8
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: Which settings should the team use to test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test the effect across several distinct problem types, including selective trait learning, broad misbehavior from narrow training, backdoor prevention and hidden transmission.
Option 2: Test mixing outside teacher-based transmission, using a setting with no teacher, a trigger-dependent bad behavior setting, and an image classification setting.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
